doc.title: Bill Allred interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 24, 2017

title: Max Corzilius, the band's angel
summary: A wealthy patron got the band booked widely, boosted its Clearwater fee, and sent a large check after playing drums on an album.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: Oh yeah. And you know you get some really fair people and then — and we were lucky enough in my band to find an angel, and this guy, his name was Max Corzilius. Max, when he worked at Dupont he figured out a way to effectively filter jet fuel. He explained it to me one time. But he had the presence of mind at a certain point when he got a little older, he left Dupont and took his patent with him and opened up his own factory to make © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

this filtered jet fuel, so he became immensely rich, oh my God. So he heard us one time and he said, “Boy I love your band,” he said, “do you guys ever play out here at Smithsonian?” I said, “No, no.” He got us booked at the Smithsonian for their Friday jazz things. And got us booked all over the east coast, Baltimore and a little place called Rock Hall where they had a jazz club. And when we started playing the jazz festival in Clearwater — we’re not there this year but I mean every, for a long time we played it. And Max, he went to the Clearwater people and he says, “Tell you what,” he said, “you need sponsors, right?” They said yes. Usually they’re hunting them. He said, “Well I’ll give you twenty thousand dollars” but he said, “half has to go to the Bill Allred band. So we got a huge raise that lasted for five or six years. So we want to do something for him because he’s kind of a hack drummer. I mean he’s not a good drummer but he could keep time you know. So I called him up I said, “Max” I said, “we’re doing an album.” And I said, “Would you like to play on a couple of tracks?” And I’m sure he said, “Yes!” But he said, “I don’t know.” I said, “Max, you’ll be fine.” I said, “Warren, our drummer, will be right there with you.” So we recorded it, he’s on two tracks, did a good job, just kept time, that’s all we wanted you know. And I sent him a paycheck for recording scale for what he did which then was like $320 or something like that. And strictly above board you know. And he was so thrilled I guess his wife said he framed it and put it in his den, the check. Because I wondered why it never cleared. So I opened the mail one day and I get a check for twelve thousand dollars from him. And I called him and I said, “Max, it’s got to be a mistake here.” He said, “No, no. I understand you guys record these albums and make no money until you pay off the production.” That’s what we did. And we were traveling enough then that we’d get things paid off quickly. And he said, “This will help you pay off your album.” I said it’s about three quarters. And he wouldn’t take it back. But he died on us about seven years ago, and that was a big loss, and not being too monetarily oriented but —
Yeah, that’s an angel for sure.
But anyway he was great, neat guy, and his wife, she died as well a few years later. But they’re out there.
